title: Why Do We Tell Ourselves Scary Stories About AI?
gist: Yuval Noah Harari's much-repeated anecdote about GPT-4 hiring a Taskrabbit worker and lying about a vision impairment to beat a captcha was told on Morning Joe, The Daily Show and in a New York Times op-ed, and is called wildly misleading. The piece's argument is that stories about AI acquiring survival drives, resource-grabbing and manipulation reveal more about human narrative instincts than about what language models actually do.

insights.claim: Historian Yuval Noah Harari's widely circulated story that GPT-4 hired a human on Taskrabbit and lied about having a vision impairment in order to get a captcha solved is characterized as wildly misleading.
insights.speaker: Amanda Gefter
insights.so_what: The single most-cited public evidence of AI deception is contested at the factual level — discount AI-risk narratives built on it.

insights.claim: In Harari's fall 2024 telling on Morning Joe, OpenAI tested GPT-4 on captcha puzzles, the model failed, and it then used Taskrabbit to get a human to solve the puzzle while denying being a robot.
insights.speaker: Amanda Gefter
insights.so_what: Know the exact chain of the canonical deception anecdote before it is used as an input to AI policy or risk assessments.
insights.quote: And GPT-4 told the human, ‘No, I’m not a robot, I have a vision impairment so I can’t see the captcha puzzles. This is why I need help.’
insights.locator: In fall 2024, the best-selling author and historian

insights.claim: Harari draws the conclusion from the captcha episode that AI is already able not just to invent things but also to manipulate people — an escalation from capability to intent.
insights.speaker: Amanda Gefter
insights.so_what: Watch how quickly capability demos get reframed as agency claims — that leap drives regulatory momentum more than the underlying evidence does.
insights.quote: So it is already able not just to invent things, it’s also able to manipulate people.
insights.locator: And the human was duped and did it for it.

insights.claim: Tales of AI developing the will to survive, commandeer resources and manipulate people say more about the humans telling them than about the language models they purport to describe.
insights.speaker: Amanda Gefter
insights.so_what: Anthropomorphic AI-risk framing is a cultural signal, not a technical one — separate it from real model-capability data when sizing AI regulatory risk.
insights.quote: Our tales of AI developing the will to survive, commandeer resources, and manipulate people say more about us than they do about language models.
insights.locator: Why Do We Tell Ourselves Scary Stories About AI?

insights.claim: The same unchecked AI anecdote propagated across a talk show, The Daily Show and a New York Times op-ed, showing how a high-status public intellectual's story can circulate through elite media without factual challenge.
insights.speaker: Amanda Gefter
insights.so_what: Elite-media repetition, not verification, is what sets the public AI-risk baseline that policymakers respond to.
insights.locator: When Harari told the same story on The Daily Show

insights.claim: The audience reaction to the captcha story was visceral rather than analytical: The Daily Show audience gasped and Morning Joe co-host Jonathan Lemire called the example terrifying.
insights.speaker: Amanda Gefter
insights.so_what: Fear responses to AI anecdotes are emotional and immediate, which is why narrative control matters more than technical accuracy in the AI policy debate.
insights.quote: “I’ll just say that example strikes me as terrifying,” co-host Jonathan Lemire said.
